content: Venom immunotherapy (VIT) is a treatment designed to prevent allergic reactions to insect stings in individuals who have previously experienced such reactions. This therapy involves the use of venom extracted from insects, such as bees, wasps, or ants, and is administered either subcutaneously (under the skin) or sublingually (under the tongue). The goal of VIT is to desensitize the immune system to the venom, thereby reducing the likelihood of severe allergic responses to future stings. A systematic review was conducted to evaluate the efficacy and safety of VIT. The review included six randomized controlled trials and one quasi-randomized controlled trial, with a total of 392 participants. These trials involved both children and adults who had experienced systemic or large local allergic reactions to insect stings. The primary outcome assessed was the prevention of systemic allergic reactions to subsequent stings, whether accidental or intentionally administered during the trials. The results demonstrated that VIT is highly effective in reducing the risk of systemic allergic reactions. Among participants treated with VIT, only 2.7% (3 out of 113) experienced a systemic allergic reaction to a sting, compared to 39.8% (37 out of 93) of untreated participants. This corresponds to a risk ratio (RR) of 0.10, with a 95% confidence interval (CI) of 0.03 to 0.28. The efficacy of VIT was consistent across the studies, and no specific patient group or treatment method was identified as having significantly different outcomes. However, due to the rarity of fatal reactions to insect stings, the review could not confirm whether VIT prevents fatal outcomes. In addition to preventing systemic allergic reactions, VIT was also effective in reducing large local reactions to stings. Five studies reported this outcome, with a risk ratio of 0.41 (95% CI 0.24 to 0.69) based on 112 follow-up stings. Furthermore, VIT was shown to improve quality of life, with a mean difference of 1.21 points on a 7-point scale (95% CI 0.75 to 1.67) in favor of the treatment. However, the review also identified a significant risk of systemic adverse reactions associated with VIT. Among participants treated with VIT, 9.3% (14 out of 150) experienced systemic reactions to the treatment, compared to 0.7% (1 out of 135) of those who received placebo or no treatment. This corresponds to a risk ratio of 8.16 (95% CI 1.53 to 43.46). An analysis of 11 observational studies further revealed that systemic adverse reactions occurred in 14.2% (131 out of 921) of participants treated with bee venom VIT and 2.8% (8 out of 289) of those treated with wasp venom VIT. In conclusion, venom immunotherapy using extracted insect venom is an effective treatment for preventing allergic reactions to insect stings and can significantly improve quality of life for affected individuals. However, the therapy carries a small but notable risk of systemic adverse reactions, which should be carefully considered when deciding on treatment.
